msgs.title: After every sell-off, the explanations pile up by the hour.
msgs.pub:
After every sell-off, the explanations pile up by the hour.

A medieval monk, William of Ockham, gave his name to a rule: do not add causes you do not need.

Today one stock drops and you get a theory about the Fed and another about insiders.

Most of the time the reason is plain. More sellers than buyers at that price.

The chart does not lie. The stories around it often do.

Sometimes there is a hidden cause. Someone always knows.

I still wait for proof before I trade the complicated story.

The simplest reason is usually the cheapest one to believe.

msgs.title: Your trading plan was written by a hopeful version of you.
msgs.pub:
Your trading plan was written by a hopeful version of you.

La Rochefoucauld put it in one line: we promise according to our hopes and perform according to our fears.

On Sunday the stop sits at a clean level and the target is far away.

On Tuesday the stock dips toward the stop, and the hand moves the stop lower.

The plan was fine. The person running it was scared.

So I write my plans for the scared version now, with smaller size and stops I can live with.

Size the trade for the person who will press the button.

msgs.title: Most portfolios die from too many good ideas.
msgs.pub:
Most portfolios die from too many good ideas.

The Greek poet Archilochus left one line: the fox knows many things, the hedgehog knows one big thing.

Retail traders love to play fox, with a new theme every week and a new name every dip.

The hedgehog rolls into a ball and waits.

The fox wins some weeks. I have been the fox, and it felt smart.

Over a full cycle, the busy account pays the spread and the tax again and again.

Know one big thing about your position and let the noise roll off.

Clever is expensive.

msgs.title: Every bottom looks obvious once the chart is finished.
msgs.pub:
Every bottom looks obvious once the chart is finished.

Kierkegaard wrote in his journal that life is understood backwards but must be lived forwards.

Markets work exactly like that.

On the chart, the low is a clean V and the entry sits right there.

In real time that day was red and loud, and options buyers were paying anything for puts.

I study old charts every weekend. Hindsight teaches a lot.

Your account only lives in the days before you knew.

So I size every position for the fog.

msgs.title: Every cycle crowns a few market heroes.
msgs.pub:
Every cycle crowns a few market heroes.

Retail buys what they buy and repeats what they say on TV.

Then one bad year arrives.

The same people who worshipped them stop reading them at all.

The hero barely changed. The tape changed under them.

Following a person is renting their conviction, and the rent runs out at the worst moment.

I keep my own written reasons for every position, so nobody can take them away when the idol falls.

msgs.title: Fear in markets can come from almost nothing.
msgs.pub:
Fear in markets can come from almost nothing.

A rumor at lunch can take billions off the screen by the close.

And some of the biggest rallies started in the worst news of their decade.

Mood has no address.

It shows up from nowhere and leaves the same way.

So I stopped waiting for the news to feel good before buying.

By the time the headlines turn kind, the smart money has already filled.

msgs.title: Watch what an investor hates and you learn more than from what they own.
msgs.pub:
Watch what an investor hates and you learn more than from what they own.

The trader who mocks every gold buyer usually sold their gold too early.

The one who calls every rally a bull trap has often been short for months.

Hate is a position report.

It tells you exactly where it hurts.

When I catch myself sneering at a trade, I check my own book first.

Most of the time the anger is about money I did not make.
